Now, however, she wished it had not occurred. She suspected that he had taken too freely of Mr. Weston's excellent wine, and was certain he would be inclined to talk foolishly.

Hoping to check him by the example of her own behaviour, she prepared at once to discuss the weather and the evening with the utmost composure and seriousness. Yet scarcely had she begun, scarcely had they gone through the sweep-gate and drawn alongside the other carriage, before her topic was broken off, her hand caught, her attention claimed, and Mr. Elton was positively declaring his passion for her. He seized the invaluable opportunity to avow feelings she must surely know already; hoping, fearing, worshipping, prepared to die at her refusal, yet persuading himself that his fervent attachment, incomparable love, and unprecedented ardour must produce some response. In brief, he was thoroughly determined to be seriously accepted with as little delay as possible. It was indeed true. Without hesitation, without apology, and with scarcely any visible bashfulness, Mr. Elton, whom she regarded as Harriet's lover, was announcing himself her own. She attempted to interrupt him, but uselessly; he insisted on continuing until all was said. Angry though she felt, the circumstances made her resolve to govern herself when her turn came. Half this absurdity must, she thought, be due to wine, and she could therefore hope it would disappear with the hour. Accordingly, mingling gravity with playfulness in a manner she thought suitable to his half-and-half condition, she answered:

“Mr. Elton, I am exceedingly astonished. Such words to me! You forget yourself; you mistake me for my friend. I shall gladly carry any message to Miss Smith, but pray address no more of this to me.”

“Miss Smith! A message to Miss Smith! What could she possibly intend?” He echoed her expressions with so confident a tone and so ostentatious an affectation of surprise that she could not refrain from answering sharply:

“Mr. Elton, your behaviour is extraordinary beyond anything! There is only one explanation I can give it. You are not yourself, or you could never speak to me, or about Harriet, in this fashion. Restrain yourself sufficiently to say nothing further, and I shall try to forget it.”

But Mr. Elton had consumed only enough wine to raise his spirits, not to cloud his understanding. He knew his intentions perfectly. Having indignantly rejected her suspicion as a serious injury, and briefly mentioned his esteem for Miss Smith as her friend, while confessing astonishment that Miss Smith should enter the discussion at all, he returned to his own passion and pressed eagerly for a favourable reply.

And all the time he pretended Peter had told him these things by letter, but that was a lie. Every last one had come from the young numbskull we took in the canoe to the steamboat.

Then Mary Jane brought out the letter her father had left, and the king read it aloud, crying as he went. It left the house and three thousand dollars in gold to the girls; to Harvey and William it gave the tanyard, which was doing well, some more houses and land worth about seven thousand, and another three thousand in gold. It also explained where the six thousand in cash lay hidden in the cellar. These two cheats announced they'd fetch it, so everything could be plain and above-board, and ordered me to bring a candle. We closed the cellar door behind us, found the bag, and poured the money on the floor. All those gold pieces made a lovely sight. How the king's eyes glittered! He clapped the duke on the shoulder and says:

“Oh, this ain't grand or anything, is it? No, I suppose not! Why, Bilji, this beats the Nonesuch, don't it?”

The duke agreed. They ran their hands through the gold, sifted it between their fingers, and let it fall jingling on the floor. The king says:

“There ain't no doubt about it. Being a rich dead man's brothers, and agents for foreign heirs that's been left fortunes, is the trade for us, Bilge. This is what trusting Providence brings you. Best way there is, in the end. I've tried every way, and none beats it.”

Most folks would have been content with that pile and accepted the amount without question. But not them; they had to count. And when they counted, it was four hundred and fifteen dollars short. The king says:

“Dern him! What's he gone and done with that four hundred and fifteen?”

They fretted awhile and searched everywhere. Then the duke says:

“Well, he was mighty sick. Likely he counted wrong; I reckon that's it. We'd best leave it alone and say nothing. We can spare the difference.”

“Oh, shucks, of course we can spare it. I ain't worried about that. It's having the count right that matters. We want everything awful honest and open here, don't we? We want to carry the money upstairs and count it where everyone can see; then there's nothing to raise suspicion. But with the dead man saying there's six thousand dollars, we don't want to—”

She would live among people who loved her and possessed sounder judgment than her own, secluded enough to remain safe and sufficiently occupied to be cheerful. She would neither be drawn into temptation nor left idle for temptation to discover. Respectability and happiness would be hers; and Emma acknowledged her as the most fortunate creature alive in having inspired such constant, enduring affection in such a man—or, if not the most fortunate, second only to herself.

Harriet's engagements with the Martins naturally drew her away, and her visits to Hartfield grew less frequent. This was no cause for regret. Her intimacy with Emma must diminish, their friendship settling into a quieter goodwill; fortunately, the change which propriety and necessity demanded seemed already to have begun, gently and by the most natural degrees.

Before September ended, Emma accompanied Harriet to church and watched her give her hand to Robert Martin with a satisfaction no recollection could diminish, not even those associated with Mr. Elton as he stood before them. Perhaps at that moment she scarcely regarded Mr. Elton except as the clergyman whose next blessing at the altar might be pronounced over herself. Of the three couples, Robert Martin and Harriet Smith, the last to become engaged, were the first to marry.

Jane Fairfax had left Highbury already and returned to the comforts of her cherished home with the Campbells. The Mr. Churchills were likewise in town, and nothing remained but to wait for November.

The intervening month was the time Emma and Mr. Knightley had selected, so far as they dared. They had resolved that the wedding should take place while John and Isabella remained at Hartfield, thus permitting the planned fortnight's journey to the seaside. John and Isabella approved, as did all their other friends. But Mr. Woodhouse—how could they secure Mr. Woodhouse's consent? He had never spoken of their marriage except as something far in the future.

At the first approach to the subject, his misery nearly destroyed their hopes. A second mention, however, caused him less suffering. He began to believe that it would happen and that he could not stop it, a most encouraging advance towards resignation. Still, he was unhappy—so plainly unhappy, indeed, that his daughter's resolution deserted her. She could not endure his distress or the knowledge that he imagined himself neglected. Both the Mr. Knightleys assured her that once the wedding was over, his suffering would soon pass as well; and although her reason almost accepted their assurance, she wavered. She could not go forward.
